title: Shoot System
summary: The shoot system is the aerial part developed from the plumule: stem, branches, leaves, flowers, fruits and seeds. The stem grows up and towards light (positively phototropic, negatively geotropic), has nodes and internodes, bears leaves, vegetative buds (terminal and axillary) and floral buds, and has no cap. Stem versus root: the stem develops from the plumule, is green when young, has nodes and internodes, bears buds and leaves, lateral branches are exogenous (arise from outer layers) while lateral roots are endogenous (arise from the pericycle).

The shoot apex has the tunica (outer 1-3 layers, divide anticlinally, give the epidermis and surface growth) and the corpus (inner mass dividing in all planes; gives procambium for vascular tissue and ground meristem, and leaf primordia). Branches arise exogenously from axillary buds.

Modifications of stem: Underground (nodes, scaly non-green leaves and buds identify them as stems; perennating and food-storing): rhizome (ginger, turmeric), corm (yam, gladiolus, colocasia), bulb (onion) and tuber (potato with eyes). Sub-aerial (weak stems for vegetative propagation): runner (grass, Oxalis), stolon (jasmine, mint, strawberry), offset (water hyacinth, water lettuce) and sucker (chrysanthemum). Aerial: stem tendrils (grape vine; climbing), thorns (citrus, Duranta; protection), phylloclade (Opuntia; green flattened stem for photosynthesis and water storage; leaves reduced to spines) and cladode (Asparagus; a phylloclade of one or two internodes). Functions of stem: conduction of water, minerals and food; support and orientation of leaves; bearing flowers and fruits; storage, perennation, vegetative propagation (rose, sugarcane), photosynthesis, protection and climbing.

Dicot stem (sunflower): epidermis with cuticle and multicellular hairs; cortex with hypodermis (collenchyma), general cortex (parenchyma) and endodermis (starch sheath); stele with pericycle (with sclerenchyma patches), vascular bundles arranged in a ring that are conjoint, collateral and open with endarch xylem, medullary rays and pith. Monocot stem (maize): epidermis without hairs; sclerenchymatous hypodermis; undifferentiated ground tissue; numerous scattered vascular bundles that are conjoint, collateral and closed with a bundle sheath, xylem in a Y shape and a water cavity formed by the disintegrated protoxylem; no secondary growth.

Differences between dicot and monocot stems: hairs present or absent; hypodermis collenchymatous or sclerenchymatous; ground tissue differentiated or undifferentiated; bundles in a ring or scattered, open or closed; bundle sheath absent or present; water cavity absent or present; secondary growth present or absent. Stem versus root: the stem has cuticle and multicellular hairs, a wide cortex, endarch xylem and a pith, while the root has no cuticle, unicellular root hairs, exarch xylem and a fixed number of radial bundles.

Secondary growth (dicot stem only): fascicular cambium and interfascicular cambium (from medullary rays) join to form a cambial ring that cuts secondary xylem inwards (more) and secondary phloem outwards; cork cambium (phellogen) develops in the cortex and cuts phellem (cork, suberised) outside and phelloderm inside; the periderm (phellogen, phellem and phelloderm) replaces the epidermis; lenticels allow gas exchange; all tissues outside the cork cambium form the bark. Annual rings are formed by spring (early) wood (light, wide vessels) and autumn (late) wood (dark, narrow vessels); counting rings is dendrochronology. Sapwood is the outer, light, functional wood; heartwood is the inner, dark, non-functional wood with gums, resins and tannins, harder and more durable.

A leaf is a lateral flattened appendage of the stem at a node with an axillary bud. Parts: leaf base (stipules in dicots, sheath in monocots), petiole (sessile if absent) and lamina with midrib and veins. Venation: reticulate (dicots; unicostate as in peepal, multicostate as in grape vine) and parallel (monocots). Simple leaves have a single lamina; compound leaves have leaflets attached to the rachis or the petiole end (pinnately compound: unipinnate, bipinnate, tripinnate; palmately compound: bifoliate to multifoliate); an axillary bud is present at the base of a leaf but not of a leaflet. Phyllotaxy: alternate (china rose, mango), opposite decussate (Calotropis, tulsi) or superposed (guava), and whorled (Nerium).

Leaf modifications: tendrils (prickly poppy, pea), spines (Opuntia, Aloe, Argemone), phyllode (Australian acacia, flattened petiole), pitcher (Nepenthes) and bladder (Utricularia) for trapping insects. Heterophylly: different types of leaves on the same plant (water chestnut, Limnophila). Functions: photosynthesis, gas exchange, transpiration, guttation and special functions.

Internal structure: dicot leaves are dorsiventral (stomata mostly on the lower epidermis, palisade and spongy mesophyll), monocot leaves are isobilateral (stomata on both surfaces, only spongy mesophyll, bulliform cells in the upper epidermis that curl the leaf to reduce transpiration). Vascular bundles of the leaf are conjoint, collateral and closed, surrounded by a bundle sheath. Kidney-shaped guard cells in dicots and dumbbell-shaped in monocots. Hydathodes are water stomata at vein endings near the margins (guttation: liquid water with salts, in humid climate); stomata lose water as vapour and are present all over, opening and closing with light.

A flower is a modified shoot: pedicel, thalamus, calyx (sepals; protection), corolla (petals; attract insects), androecium (stamens with filament, anther and connective) and gynoecium (carpels each with ovary, style and stigma). Variations: complete or incomplete; bisexual or unisexual (monoecious such as cucumber, dioecious such as papaya); actinomorphic (mustard), zygomorphic (pea) or asymmetric (Canna); stamens monadelphous (china rose), diadelphous (pea), polyadelphous (lemon), syngenesious (sunflower), epipetalous (brinjal), didynamous (tulsi) and tetradynamous (mustard); gynoecium monocarpellary (pea) or polycarpellary, syncarpous (tomato) or apocarpous (lotus); hypogynous (superior ovary; china rose, mustard), perigynous (peach) and epigynous (inferior ovary; sunflower, cucumber).

Placentation: marginal (pea), axile (china rose, tomato), parietal (mustard, cucumber), basal (sunflower), free central (Dianthus, Primula). Inflorescence: arrangement of flowers on the peduncle; racemose (axis grows; flowers acropetal: raceme, spike, catkin, spadix, corymb, umbel, capitulum) and cymose (axis ends in a flower; basipetal: monochasial, dichasial, polychasial). Special types: hypanthodium (hollow receptacle with male and female flowers on the inner wall, ostiole; fig, peepal), cyathium (Euphorbia; a cup-shaped involucre with one female flower surrounded by male flowers) and verticillaster (clusters of sessile flowers at each node; Ocimum, Salvia).

A true fruit is a ripened ovary; the pericarp (epicarp, mesocarp, endocarp) develops from the ovary wall. False fruits involve other parts (apple and pear: thalamus; fig: receptacle). Parthenocarpic fruits develop without fertilisation (banana, grapes). Kinds: simple (legume, siliqua, follicle, capsule, caryopsis, nut, drupe, berry, pepo, hesperidium, pome), aggregate (etaerio: raspberry, strawberry, custard apple) and composite (sorosis: pineapple, mulberry, jackfruit; syconus: fig). Edible parts: mango, mesocarp; coconut, endosperm; wheat, endosperm; orange, juicy hairs of the endocarp; cashew nut, peduncle and cotyledons.

vsa: Explain the term 'Hypanthodium' with an example.
An inflorescence with a hollow, cup-shaped receptacle with an apical opening (ostiole); male and female flowers lie on the inner wall; e.g. fig and peepal.
October 2025
What is a phylloclade? Give an example.
A green, flattened or cylindrical fleshy stem that photosynthesises and stores water; e.g. Opuntia (leaves are reduced to spines).
Differentiate between a simple and a compound leaf (two points).
A simple leaf has an undivided lamina (or incisions not reaching the midrib); a compound leaf has leaflets, incisions reaching the midrib, and an axillary bud only at the base of the whole leaf.
Write the difference between sapwood and heartwood (two points).
Sapwood is outer, light and functional; heartwood is inner, dark, hard, non-functional and more durable.
Distinguish between racemose and cymose inflorescences (two points).
In racemose the main axis grows continuously and flowers are acropetal; in cymose the axis ends in a flower and flowers are basipetal.
Differentiate between true fruit and false fruit.
A true fruit develops from the ovary alone (mango); a false fruit includes other floral parts such as the thalamus (apple).
Mention two functions of the stem other than conduction.
Storage of food (potato) and vegetative propagation (rose, sugarcane).
What are hydathodes? Write their function.
Water pores at the vein endings near leaf margins that exude liquid water with salts (guttation) in humid conditions.
What is dendrochronology?
Determining the age of a tree by counting its annual growth rings.
Name the types of stamens in (a) pea (b) mustard.
(a) Diadelphous. (b) Tetradynamous.
sa: With the help of a neat labelled diagram briefly explain the verticillaster type of inflorescence. Give one example.

A series of condensed dichasial cymes at each node with a cluster of sessile flowers in the axil of the opposite leaves, giving a whorl-like cluster all around the node; e.g. Ocimum (tulsi) and Salvia. (Draw an axis with nodes, each node showing a whorl of sessile flowers.)
With the help of a neat labelled diagram briefly explain the hypanthodium inflorescence. Give one suitable example.
The receptacle is a fleshy, hollow cup with a small apical opening (ostiole); the inner wall bears male flowers near the opening and female flowers below; e.g. fig and peepal.
Differentiate between the dicot stem and the monocot stem (any three points).

Dicot: hypodermis collenchymatous, vascular bundles in a ring and open, secondary growth present. Monocot: sclerenchymatous hypodermis, bundles scattered, closed with bundle sheath and a water cavity, no secondary growth.
Differentiate between a stoma and a hydathode (three points).
Stomata are all over the leaf, lose water as vapour and open or close with light; hydathodes are at vein endings near margins, lose liquid water with salts and are always open.
Arrangement of leaves on a stem: alternate (one leaf per node; china rose, mango), opposite (pairs; decussate in tulsi and superposed in guava) and whorled (more than two per node; Nerium).
Explain the modification of leaves with examples.
Tendrils (climb; pea), spines (protect and reduce transpiration; Opuntia), phyllode (flattened petiole; Australian acacia), pitcher (Nepenthes) and bladder (Utricularia) for trapping insects.
Explain the types of placentation with one example each.
Marginal (pea), axile (china rose), parietal (mustard), basal (sunflower) and free central (Dianthus).
Describe the types of vegetative modifications of subaerial stems.
Runner (grass), stolon (jasmine), offset (water hyacinth) and sucker (chrysanthemum): they lie on or partly in the soil, strike roots at nodes and propagate vegetatively.
la: Identify the modified plant part in the following: (1) Rhizome of ginger (2) Carrot (3) Spines of Opuntia (4) Thorns of Citrus (5) Phylloclade of Opuntia.

(1) Underground stem (storage and perennation). (2) Tap root (conical, storage). (3) Modified leaves (reduce transpiration and protect). (4) Modified axillary bud, a stem (protection). (5) Modified stem (photosynthesis and water storage).
Describe the secondary growth in a dicot stem.

Fascicular and interfascicular cambium form a ring that adds secondary xylem inside and secondary phloem outside, with more xylem; cork cambium in the cortex forms cork outside and phelloderm inside; the periderm replaces the epidermis; lenticels aerate; bark is all the tissue outside the cork cambium; spring and autumn wood form annual rings.
Describe the internal structure of a dicot stem.

Epidermis with hairs, hypodermis of collenchyma, parenchymatous cortex and endodermis (starch sheath), pericycle with sclerenchyma, vascular bundles in a ring (conjoint, collateral, open, endarch xylem), medullary rays and pith.
Differentiate between the dicot leaf and the monocot leaf.

Dicot leaf is dorsiventral with stomata mostly on the lower surface, palisade and spongy tissue and no bulliform cells; monocot leaf is isobilateral with stomata on both surfaces, only spongy mesophyll and bulliform cells on the upper epidermis.
Explain the various types of stem modifications with examples.
Underground: rhizome, corm, bulb, tuber; subaerial: runner, stolon, offset, sucker; aerial: tendril, thorn, phylloclade and cladode, with their functions.
Describe the major kinds of fruits with examples.

Simple fruits (dry dehiscent such as pea legume, mustard siliqua; dry indehiscent such as wheat caryopsis; fleshy such as mango drupe, tomato berry, cucumber pepo, orange hesperidium, apple pome), aggregate (strawberry) and composite fruits (pineapple, fig).
